heading: 451 years as someone else's colony
body: Goa's history is set apart from the rest of the Indian mainland by a single fact: it spent longer under continuous European colonial rule than almost anywhere else in Asia. Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate for Portugal in 1510, and for the next four and a half centuries it served as the capital of the entire Portuguese empire east of the Cape of Good Hope — the administrative hub through which horses, spices and slaves moved between East Africa, India, and as far as Japan, and the seat of the Viceroy of Portuguese India. Old Goa, the original colonial capital, grew so grand that contemporaries called it the "Rome of the East" before repeated epidemics forced the administration to relocate roughly ten kilometers west to what became Panaji in the 17th century.

That long Portuguese presence also produced one of the harsher chapters in the subcontinent's colonial record: the Goa Inquisition, established in 1560 and running, with one four-year suspension, until 1812. Portuguese colonial authorities used it to enforce conversion to Catholicism, destroying Hindu temples and idols, banning Hindu religious practice and Konkani cultural expression, and in documented cases removing children from families to be raised Catholic. Historians differ on the exact scale of the Inquisition's violence, but its documentary record and its lasting effect on Goa's religious demographics — still visibly different from any neighboring Indian state — are not in dispute.

Portuguese rule did not end when the rest of India became independent in 1947; Portugal held onto Goa for another fourteen years, and it took an Indian military action in December 1961 to end what is now officially marked as 451 years of colonial rule, commemorated annually as Goa Liberation Day. That extra decade and a half of separation is part of why Goa's built environment — laterite churches, Portuguese-tiled townhouses, fort chapels — reads as distinctly apart from anywhere else on the Indian map.

The sites on Goa's map track that arc: the Bijapur-era fortifications Albuquerque seized, the churches and administrative core of Old Goa built during Portuguese rule, and the later colonial townscape of Panaji.
